notes.title: Coding agent

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The loop, the verifier and where these agents actually fail — SWE-bench (arXiv 2310.06770)

  • Why the harness matters more than the model here — Anthropic: building effective agents

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • coding agents — the plan/edit/test loop, repo-map context, SWE-agent patterns.

What this note adds: the run sheet. Not what a coding agent is — which decisions this brief forces, in the order the round will ask for them, and what makes this problem different from every other one in §14.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

A real verifier exists, and it is the whole design. Tests, the compiler and the linter give ground truth for free, which inverts four decisions that go the other way everywhere else in this section.

Three facts define the problem: the environment grades the work; the action space is a filesystem and a shell, so it can't be typed; and the task is long, so cost is quadratic and the context fills.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §1 Is there a verifier Yes — tests. Say it in the first two minutes. Every line below follows from it.
2 §2 Model or harness Harness. Repo map, file tools, test runner. The model is fixed; the context you hand it isn't.
3 §3 Adaptive loop, plan, or ReWOO Adaptive. Step three depends on what the tests said. Plans die at the first failing test.
4 §11 Which boundary code runs behind Fresh microVM, egress denied, repo mounted. Model-written code is the untrusted thing.
5 §4 Shell or typed action space Shell. The action space can't be enumerated. Which is why step 4 is non-negotiable.
6 §12 What counts as the score The test suite. pass@k is honest here. Tests select the winning attempt.
7 §12 Which layer gates End-to-end, every commit — uniquely affordable. The repo already is a resettable graded world.
8 §10 Which factor of steps² Cache the accumulated prefix; files dominate g. Long runs, large tool results.
9 §10 Route by step or cascade Route by phase: reads cheap, patches frontier. ~70/30 split; phases, not steps, to keep caches warm.
10 §13 The versioned unit Pin hard. Prompts here are tuned to a snapshot. Coding prompts are the most model-specific there are.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

The verifier inverts pass@k. This is the one design in §14 where "succeeded at least once in k attempts" is the honest metric, because the test suite picks the winner. It stops being honest the moment the agent commits its own work unreviewed — so which metric applies is a statement about the workflow, not the agent.

Context is files, and files are enormous. The context budget fight here isn't conversation history, it's tool results: one cat of a large file can cost more than ten steps of reasoning. That makes a repo map and targeted reads a cost decision as much as a quality one.

Tests verify what tests cover. The verifier is real and partial. An agent that makes the suite green by weakening an assertion has satisfied the grader, so the gates that matter are the ones tests don't express — did it touch files outside scope, did it delete a test, how many steps and how much did it cost.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Treating the test suite as the whole eval. Green tests say the patch is acceptable; they say nothing about the agent reading forty files it didn't need, taking sixty steps where six would do, or costing four times the last release to reach the same verdict. Those regress silently precisely because the headline metric stays green — so cost per successful task and steps per task belong on the dashboard beside the pass rate.

5. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • coding agents — the pattern this run sheet sequences.

notes.title: Support agent that takes actions

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Consistency on a rule-bound support domain, measured — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

  • The excessive-agency class this design spends most of its time bounding — OWASP LLM06:2025

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • customer-support and rpa agents — the support pattern, retrieval grounding, escalation.

What this note adds: the run sheet. The ordering that falls out of one fact — there is no verifier and the actions are real — and the three answers the generic decisions don't give you.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

No verifier, real side effects, and a customer waiting. Nothing checks the answer before it lands, the actions move money or change accounts, and the latency class is interactive.

That combination is the hardest one in §14: the coding agent has a grader, the research agent has no side effects, and this has neither protection.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §1 Is there a verifier No. Confidence and escalation replace it. Say it early; it explains everything below.
2 §1 Autonomy level Per-action, by reversibility × cost. Reads autonomous, refunds gated.
3 §11 Which leg of the trifecta Break exfiltration — draft, don't send. Customer text is untrusted content.
4 §4 Read vs write tools Default-deny on writes, idempotency keys. A retried refund is the expensive bug.
5 §11 Where the approval gate sits Tool layer, on the effect, threshold by amount. And audit the graph for composed sends.
6 §11 Whose authority Delegated, so the agent can't exceed the agent. Confused deputy is live here.
7 §4 Escalation as a tool or a terminal state A callable tool — it's the substitute verifier. Escalation is the product, not a failure.
8 §12 What counts as the score End state, pass^k, plus a separate harm rate. One refund missed ≠ one refund doubled.
9 §12 Which production signal Escalation rate — the business already tracks it. Same number for canary and for the board.
10 §9 Where the time goes Short runs, so output tokens lead, not steps². Inverts the cost story from the research agent.
11 §10 Route by step Classification routes down; the action step doesn't. The usual first win, and the usual over-reach.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

Confidence-based escalation is what replaces the verifier. With no ground truth, the design's substitute is a threshold on the agent's own uncertainty plus structural checks — does the cited policy exist, is the order id real, is the amount within the customer's history. Escalation is the safety net, so the escalation rate is a health metric rather than an embarrassment, and driving it to zero is a bug.

The approval threshold is a money number, not an engineering one. "Refunds under £50 auto-approve" comes from finance's tolerance for loss, not from model confidence. Naming that in the round is what shows the decision belongs to the business, and it's also what keeps the gate rare enough to be read rather than rubber-stamped.

Two scores, not one. A missed resolution is a support ticket; a duplicate refund is money gone and a customer-facing incident. Averaging them into a single success rate hides exactly the failure that matters, and it makes it impossible to ship at 80% — which you otherwise could.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Grading the final message instead of the ledger. The agent's closing sentence says the refund is processed; the grader matches it against a reference answer and scores it correct; the refund never landed because a tool call returned a validation error the agent summarised as success. The eval rises, support volume rises with it, and the two numbers never meet. Assert on the system the agent was supposed to change — the transcript is a claim, the ledger is the fact.

5. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • customer-support and rpa agents — the pattern this run sheet sequences.

notes.title: Deep research agent

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The multi-agent research topology and what it costs in tokens — Anthropic: building a multi-agent research system

  • Long-horizon tool-and-reasoning tasks, and what they don't predict — GAIA (arXiv 2311.12983)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • research and analysis agents — lead/searcher topology, citation aggregation.

What this note adds: the run sheet. This is the one problem where multi-agent genuinely pays, and the ordering exists to show why — plus the two constraints that make an unbounded research loop safe to ship.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

No verifier, no side effects, and an unbounded horizon. Nothing grades the output, nothing is mutated, and the task can always justify one more search — which makes budget the only thing stopping it.

That profile is the mirror image of the support agent: there the risk was acting wrongly, here it's spending unboundedly on a question with no defined end.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §6 What justifies a second agent Yes — parallel searchers over independent subtopics. The rare brief where it's genuinely right.
2 §6 What multi-agent will cost Say the multiple out loud before they ask. Volunteering it is the credibility move.
3 §6 Delegation contract Subtopic, budget, return schema with citations. Cheap prevention of duplicated work.
4 §8 Which budgets you set Steps, tokens, wall-clock — all three, per searcher. Nothing else terminates this loop.
5 §10 Which factor of steps² The dominant cost story: long runs, big g. Fetched pages are enormous.
6 §5 Restart or keep compacting Sub-agent isolation — each searcher gets a clean window. The parent never holds every page.
7 §11 Which leg of the trifecta Content leg unavailable — it reads the open web. So exfiltration is the leg to break.
8 §12 What counts as the score Rubric judge — no ground truth exists. With the bias controls, and its ~80% ceiling.
9 §8 What it does when it can't finish Return findings so far, labelled as partial. A budget trip is the normal exit, not an error.
10 §9 What you stream Sources found, subtopics closed — not tokens. Runs are minutes; silence reads as failure.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

Termination is a design decision, not an outcome. Every other agent here stops when the task is done. Research is never done — there is always another source — so the budget is the stopping condition, and the honest framing is that you're buying a fixed amount of searching rather than an answer. That reframes the step cap from a safety net into the product's core parameter.

Citations are the substitute verifier. You can't check whether the synthesis is right, but you can check that every claim carries a source, that the source resolves, and that the quoted span exists in it. That's a deterministic check standing in for a grader, and it catches the failure that matters most — a confident synthesis of things nothing actually said.

Parallelism is what makes the horizon affordable. Searchers running concurrently turn a sum of latencies into a max, which is the only reason a twenty-source report fits a user's patience. It's also where the token multiple comes from, so the two facts belong in the same sentence when you present it.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Reaching for multi-agent because it's a research agent, without pricing it. This is the brief where multi-agent is right, which makes it the brief where candidates adopt it reflexively and can't say what it costs. The answer that lands is the one that names the topology and the token multiple and the coordination failure it introduces — duplicated work across searchers with overlapping subtopics, which is invisible because the output looks well-sourced and is actually redundant.

5. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

notes.title: Data / SQL analyst agent

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Schema grounding and the text-to-SQL failure modes — Spider: a large-scale text-to-SQL dataset (arXiv 1809.08887)

  • Why the sandbox and the query role are separate controls — OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • data and sql analyst agents — schema grounding, read-only roles, ambiguity handling.

What this note adds: the run sheet, and the distinction that makes this problem interesting — the query is verifiable and the question is not, so the design has a half-verifier and has to say which half.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

The query is checkable, the question isn't. SQL either parses and runs or it doesn't, so syntax and schema are ground truth — but whether the query answers what the user meant has no grader at all.

Add two facts: the action space is one tool with an enormous argument space, and a careless query is a cost and availability event on a shared warehouse.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §1 Is there a verifier Half. Syntax yes, intent no. Name the split. The most precise answer in §14.
2 §11 Whose authority Delegated, read-only role, row-level rules apply. The warehouse enforces, not the prompt.
3 §4 Constrain or validate after Parse and plan the query before running it. Cheapest gate available, and deterministic.
4 §5 Retrieval as a tool or fixed Schema retrieval as a tool — catalogues are huge. You can't put 4,000 columns in the prompt.
5 §10 Where the spend cap is enforced Query cost cap at the warehouse, not the prompt. A scan limit, enforced where it's counted.
6 §4 Escalation as a tool Ask a clarifying question — ambiguity is the norm. "Top customers" by revenue or by volume?
7 §12 What counts as the score Result-set equality against a reference query. Not string match — many SQL forms are correct.
8 §8 What it does when it can't finish Return the query it would run, unexecuted. A reviewable artifact beats a refusal.
9 §9 Where the time goes Tool time dominates — the warehouse is the term. Unusual: not prefill, not decode.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

Ambiguity is the workload, not an edge case. Most business questions are underspecified — which date field, which definition of active, whose timezone. An agent that guesses silently produces a confident wrong number that someone puts in a deck. So the clarifying question is a first-class tool, and the design decision is when to ask versus when to state an assumption in the output. Stating assumptions visibly is usually the better trade for a single-shot query.

Read-only is a role, not an instruction. The control is a database role that cannot write, granted to the agent's delegated session — not a prompt saying it may only select. It's the cleanest example in §14 of a control belonging where it's enforced, and it's one line of DDL.

The cost cap belongs to the warehouse. A query that scans a petabyte is a bill and an incident for everyone else on the cluster. Modern warehouses can bound bytes scanned per query, which is enforcement at the resource — exactly where §10 argues a cap binds.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Grading generated SQL by string similarity to a reference. Many correct queries look nothing alike — joins reordered, CTEs instead of subqueries, a different but equivalent filter. String comparison fails correct answers and passes some wrong ones. Run both queries against a fixture database and compare result sets; that's the grader this problem actually has, and it's available precisely because the query half is verifiable.

5. 🔗 Connections

notes.title: Voice / interview agent

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The turn-budget chain and why endpointing dominates it — OpenAI: realtime API

  • Judging a conversation you have no ground truth for — Judging LLM-as-a-judge (arXiv 2306.05685)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • voice agents — the STT/LLM/TTS chain, barge-in, turn-taking.

  • conversational and interview agents — conducting a structured conversation.

What this note adds: the run sheet, and the separation that defines this problem — conducting the conversation and evaluating it are two systems, and merging them is what breaks both.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

A sub-second budget, and a conversation that must not be graded while it's happening. The turn budget forbids a multi-step loop, and the interview's judgement has to happen after, on the transcript, where it can be slow and careful.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §9 How to spend a sub-second turn The whole design starts here. Roughly zero to one tool calls fit.
2 §1 Which rung of the ladder Conduct is a workflow, not an agent loop. A loop cannot fit the budget.
3 §9 Which transport WebRTC — audio, bidirectional, jitter-tolerant. The one place it's not over-engineering.
4 §7 What a cancel reaches Barge-in must reach TTS playback and in-flight tools. Stopping the loop alone leaves audio playing.
5 §2 Sync or async runs Conduct sync, evaluate async, after the call. The separation this problem is named for.
6 §12 What counts as the score Rubric judge on the transcript, post hoc. Where the slow, careful grading lives.
7 §12 When a judge earns its call With position and verbosity controls. It's deciding about a person.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

Conduct and evaluation are separate systems. The agent running the interview optimises for turn latency and rapport; the evaluator optimises for fairness and consistency and can take a minute. Fusing them forces the judgement into the turn budget, which makes it shallow, and it lets the evaluation leak into the conversation — the candidate hears the scoring.

Endpointing is the latency term nobody budgets for. Most of the perceived gap is the system waiting to be sure the person stopped talking. Attacking model latency while endpointing sits at 700ms is optimising the wrong term, which is the §9 argument in its most concrete form.

A person is on the other end, which raises the eval bar. A judge deciding about a human needs its bias controls in place and a human-labelled calibration set — this is the design in §14 where the ~80% agreement ceiling is a fairness question rather than a measurement one.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Designing it as an agent loop and then trying to make it fast. The turn budget admits roughly one tool call, so a plan-act-observe loop was never going to fit, and no amount of streaming or model swapping recovers it. The design starts from the budget and works backwards into a workflow — fixed steps, at most one lookup, TTS started on the first sentence rather than the full response.

5. 🔗 Connections

notes.title: Back-office workflow automation

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Where a deterministic workflow beats a loop — Anthropic: building effective agents

  • The excessive-agency boundary these automations sit on — OWASP LLM06:2025

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • workflow automation and rpa boundary — the agent/RPA boundary and hybrid shapes.

What this note adds: the run sheet, and the answer this brief usually wants — that most of it isn't an agent, and saying which parts are is the design.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

Mostly deterministic, with a few judgement steps. The process is written down, the steps are known, and two or three points need a decision a rule can't express — which is exactly the shape that rewards a hybrid and punishes an agent loop.

Nobody is waiting, so latency is irrelevant and throughput and auditability are everything.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §1 Which rung of the ladder Workflow with LLM steps, not an agent. The honest answer, and it's graded.
2 §2 Who owns the flow Code owns it; the model is called at two nodes. Determinism where determinism is possible.
3 §3 Which workflow pattern Prompt chaining, with routing at the intake. The process is the graph.
4 §2 Sync or async Async — nothing is waiting. Unlocks batch pricing and queueing.
5 §10 Batch or sync API Batch. 50% off, and the deadline is soft. The clearest batch fit in §14.
6 §7 How a run waits for a human Durable pause at each HITL checkpoint. Approvals take days here, not seconds.
7 §11 Where the approval gate sits Tool layer, on the irreversible steps. And the graph audit for composed effects.
8 §11 Audit trail Append-only record — this is a compliance surface. Back-office means auditors.
9 §8 What it does when it can't finish Route to the human queue, never guess. Unattended means nobody catches a guess.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

The design is a boundary, not a system. The interesting work is drawing the line between what code does, what an LLM step does, and what a person does — and the winning answer usually gives the model less than the brief implies. Classification, extraction from a document, a judgement on an exception: those are LLM steps. Everything else is a workflow engine.

Nobody waiting changes the economics completely. Async plus a soft deadline makes the Batch API a straight 50% saving with no trade, and it makes queue-driven scaling natural. This is the one §14 problem where latency simply isn't a design axis.

Unattended raises the bar on degradation. With no human in the loop by default, a wrong answer is silently committed to a downstream system. So the fallback is a human queue rather than a best-effort result, and the escalation rate is a throughput number the business plans staffing around.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Answering "build an agent" because the brief said automation. A written-down process with two judgement points is a workflow with two LLM calls, and proposing an autonomous loop over it adds non-determinism, cost and an audit problem to something that had none. The strong answer names the two nodes the model owns and hands the rest to code — and that reads as seniority rather than as scoping down.

5. 🔗 Connections

notes.title: Browser / computer-use agent

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What browser agents actually score on realistic web tasks — WebArena (arXiv 2307.13854)

  • The isolation boundary this problem cannot skip — Firecracker

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Parallel Tool Calling & Tool Batching — tool-call mechanics this leans on.

What this note adds: the run sheet, and the honest framing — this is the least reliable design in §14, so the answer that lands is the one that says when not to reach for it.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

An untyped action space over an interface that changes without warning. Clicks and keystrokes against UIs you don't control, where a layout change breaks a step and nothing announces it.

No verifier, real side effects if the UI can submit, and per-step reliability well below anything else here.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §4 Shell or typed action space Last resort. Use an API if one exists. The first thing to say.
2 §11 Which boundary code runs behind Isolated browser, egress allowlisted. Untrusted pages, untrusted actions.
3 §11 Which leg of the trifecta Page content is untrusted input to the model. Injection arrives in rendered text.
4 §8 Buy reliability with steps or gates Fewer steps — per-step reliability is the problem. Compounding bites hardest here.
5 §8 What is safe to retry Retry navigation, never a submit. Double-submitting a form is the classic.
6 §11 Where the approval gate sits On anything that submits or pays. The UI hides which clicks are irreversible.
7 §12 Recorded, simulated or live A pinned site fixture — live sites make evals flaky. Otherwise you measure the site, not the agent.
8 §9 Where the time goes Page loads dominate; screenshots are huge inputs. Unusual cost and latency profile.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

The action space is untyped and unstable. A shell at least has a stable contract. A UI changes underneath you with no version and no deprecation notice, so a working trajectory silently stops working — which makes the pinned fixture in step 7 less of a convenience and more of the only way to tell your regression from theirs.

Screenshots are the cost story. Vision input per step is large and it accumulates like any other context, so the steps² term here is driven by images rather than text. That argues for accessibility-tree or DOM-text representations where the site allows, which are dramatically cheaper and more stable than pixels.

Irreversibility is invisible in a UI. In a typed tool layer you can classify refund() as a write. In a browser, the same click is "the blue button", and whether it submits an order is a property of the page. That's why the gate has to be conservative and why an API, when one exists, is not merely more reliable but more auditable.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Treating it as a general-purpose capability rather than a fallback. Computer use demos beautifully and generalises to any site, which is exactly why it gets proposed where an API already exists. The senior answer is the ordering: API first, then a scripted integration, then computer use for the long tail that has neither — and a sentence about what the reliability difference between those rungs actually is.

5. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • sandboxing and isolation — the boundary this problem requires.

notes.title: Internal agent platform for many teams

headings.text: 🔁 The decisions this problem is built from

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Audience binding and the token-passthrough ban a gateway must enforce — MCP specification: authorization

  • Per-scope budgets and what a gateway returns on a trip — LiteLLM proxy: budgets and rate limits

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • agentic reference architecture — the layered architecture a platform productises.

What this note adds: the run sheet, and the inversion that makes this problem different — you are not designing an agent, you are designing the constraints other people's agents run inside.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

You don't own the agents, only the substrate. Teams write their own prompts and pick their own tools; you own the gateway, the tool registry, the tracing, the budgets and the isolation.

That means every decision you make is a default other people inherit, and every default you get wrong is wrong N times.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Decision This problem's answer Why it lands here
1 §11 Isolation by filter or construction Construction, on all four surfaces. Memory, credentials, traces, caches.
2 §11 Whose authority Delegated per team; audience-bound tokens. No platform credential reaches a team's tool.
3 §4 Adopt MCP A gateway plus a registry — the platform's core product. One place tools are published and discovered.
4 §4 When the catalogue outgrows the prompt Retrieve tools per run; the registry is the index. Hundreds of tools across teams.
5 §10 Where the spend cap is enforced Gateway, per team and per run, plus concurrency. Exposure is cap × concurrent runs.
6 §13 Provider rate limits Per-workspace reservations; priority for interactive. One team's batch job must not starve others.
7 §12 What a span must carry Standard spans, namespaced per team. Shared tracing is the platform's best feature.
8 §13 The versioned unit Two artifacts: platform's and each team's. And a model bump affects prompts you've never seen.
9 §13 Where the seam goes You are the platform — keep the state model yours. The layer with no portable equivalent.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

Your defaults are the product. Most teams will never change a setting, so whatever the platform defaults to — caching on, egress denied, writes gated, traces namespaced — is what the organisation actually gets. That makes default selection a higher-leverage activity than any feature, and it's the answer to "how do you make fifty teams' agents safe" that doesn't involve reviewing fifty agents.

A model upgrade is a breaking change you can't test. Teams tune prompts against a pinned snapshot; when you bump it, you're changing a combination for every prompt you've never seen. So the platform needs a sampled corpus of real tenant traffic to shadow against, consent to use it, and a deprecation window — which is a policy and legal question as much as an engineering one.

The tool registry is where governance actually happens. Publishing a tool is the moment to require its effect classification, its schema, its owner and its scopes. Catch it there and the gateway can enforce everything downstream; miss it and you're auditing behaviour after the fact across teams who don't report to you.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Designing an agent instead of a platform. The brief invites you to draw a loop, and the loop is the part you don't own. What's graded is whether you talk about tenancy across all four surfaces, budgets and rate-limit allocation, a tool registry with an effect classification, and what happens to fifty teams when you upgrade a model. An answer full of orchestration detail and light on those is the wrong system described well.

5. 🔗 Connections

📚 Reference Links

  • Why per-step reliability compounds into a 60% that isn't a prompt problem — Anthropic: building effective agents

  • The consistency gap a single-attempt number hides — τ-bench (arXiv 2406.12045)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • the 95% problem — why per-step success compounds multiplicatively.

  • cost modeling — where the money goes.

What this note adds: the triage order. This is the only §14 problem that is a debugging exercise, and it's graded on refusing to guess — the answer is a sequence of measurements, and every fix is named only after the measurement that justifies it.

1. 🎯 The Brief in One Line

A number with no attribution, and an invitation to guess. Two complaints, no traces offered, and the failure mode being tested is whether you start proposing fixes before you know which step fails or which term the money is in.

2. 🗺️ The Run Sheet

# Step What you're establishing Decision it resolves
1 Ask what 60% means Metric and k. pass@1 or pass^k? §12 What counts as the score
2 Ask what's graded Final message, or the end state? Same — most 60%s grade the transcript.
3 Read traces, classify failures Which step, and into how many buckets. §12 Which layer gates
4 Get the step distribution p50 and p99 step count per run. §10 Which factor of steps²
5 Split the bill Prefix vs growth vs output; cache hit rate. Same — the crossover says which term.
6 Then: cut steps The lever that fixes cost and reliability. §8 Fewer steps or more gates
7 Then: add a verifier Only where a cheap deterministic check exists. §8 Where the gates go
8 Then: fix caching Breakpoint on the accumulated prefix, not the system block. §10 Which cache tier
9 Then: route models Only after 6–8, and with per-tier evals. §10 Route by step or cascade
10 Gate it So the next regression is caught before users find it. §12 What blocks the merge

Steps 1–5 are measurement and cost nothing. Steps 6–9 are ordered by what they fix: cutting steps improves reliability and cost, caching improves cost and latency, routing trades quality for cost. Routing last is the whole point — it's where everyone starts.

3. 🎯 Specific to This Problem

60% over twenty steps is 97.5% per step. 0.975²⁰ ≈ 0.60, so the agent is already nearly right at every step and the loss is compounding. That single line reframes the conversation: reaching 90% needs 99.5% per step, which no prompt edit delivers, so the honest levers are fewer steps or recovery. Doing this arithmetic out loud is the strongest move available in this problem.

The two complaints usually have one cause. Long trajectories cause both — steps compound into a low success rate, and re-billed context makes cost quadratic in the same variable. So "cut steps" is frequently the single fix for both numbers, and finding that is worth more than two separate workstreams.

A failure taxonomy beats a failure rate. Forty traces hand-classified into four or five buckets — wrong tool, bad arguments, lost context, gave up early, wandered — turns one unactionable number into a ranked list. It takes an afternoon and it is the step most often skipped in favour of a prompt rewrite.

4. ⚠️ The Signature Trap

Proposing fixes before measuring. The brief is engineered to invite "I'd switch to a cheaper model and tighten the prompt" — which is a guess about both problems, and routing is the lever with the worst ratio of benefit to risk this early. Every fix you name should be preceded by the measurement that justified it, and the strongest version of this answer spends its first third on questions and refuses to skip them even when pushed.
